source_refs.note: Exercise 2.1, Question 14: x = a sec t, y = b tan t, show dy/dx = -b^2x/(a^2y) (printed sign wrong); book p. 41. No printed answers.

blocks.prompt: 14. If \(x = a\sec t\) and \(y = b\tan t\), show that \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{-b^2x}{a^2y}\).
blocks.explanation:
Parametric equations again: find \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\), then write it with \(x\) and \(y\).
Use \(\sec t = \frac{x}{a}\) and \(\tan t = \frac{y}{b}\) to remove \(t\).
Plan: differentiate, divide, substitute, compare with what we were asked to show.
steps:
Given: \(x = a\sec t\), \(y = b\tan t\).
To show: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{-b^2x}{a^2y}\) (as printed).
Method: parametric differentiation, then replace \(\sec t\) and \(\tan t\) by \(\frac{x}{a}\) and \(\frac{y}{b}\).

Differentiate w.r.t. t
\[\dfrac{dx}{dt} = a\sec t\tan t\]
\[\dfrac{dy}{dt} = b\sec^2 t\]
Why: \((\sec t)' = \sec t\tan t\), \((\tan t)' = \sec^2 t\).

Divide
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{b\sec^2 t}{a\sec t\tan t} = \dfrac{b\sec t}{a\tan t}\]
Why: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\); one \(\sec t\) cancels.

Write in x and y
\[\sec t = \dfrac{x}{a},\quad \tan t = \dfrac{y}{b}\]
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{b \cdot \frac{x}{a}}{a \cdot \frac{y}{b}} = \dfrac{b^2x}{a^2y}\]
Why: from the given equations; \(\frac{bx/a}{ay/b} = \frac{bx}{a}\cdot\frac{b}{ay}\).

Check by eliminating t
\[\sec^2 t - \tan^2 t = 1 \Rightarrow \dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\]
\[\dfrac{2x}{a^2} - \dfrac{2y}{b^2}\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{b^2x}{a^2y}\]
Why: implicit differentiation of the hyperbola gives the same result, with a plus sign.

Compare with the statement
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = +\dfrac{b^2x}{a^2y} \neq \dfrac{-b^2x}{a^2y}\]
Why: the printed result has the wrong sign, so it cannot be shown; see the correction below.
blocks.final_answer: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{b^2x}{a^2y}\). The printed result \(\frac{-b^2x}{a^2y}\) has the wrong sign.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book asks to show \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{-b^2x}{a^2y}\). For \(x = a\sec t\), \(y = b\tan t\) the correct result is \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{b^2x}{a^2y}\) (plus sign), as both methods above show. The minus sign belongs to the ellipse \(x = a\cos t\), \(y = b\sin t\), where \(\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{b\cos t}{a\sin t} = -\frac{b^2x}{a^2y}\).
